Quick Start

Source: vignettes/quick-start.Rmd
quick-start.Rmd

Overview

sciVizModules extends VizModules with a curated set of domain-specific Shiny modules for the biological, chemical, and physical sciences. Each module wraps a plotting function with scientifically meaningful defaults, axis conventions, and annotation layers, while preserving the interactivity-first philosophy of the parent package.

Every module follows the same three-function contract:

  • *InputsUI(id, data, ...) — the interactive controls.
  • *OutputUI(id) — the (Plotly) plot output.
  • *Server(id, data, ...) — the reactive logic that renders the plot.

Servers share a common signature, with data supplied as a reactive:

someModuleServer(id, data, hide.inputs = NULL, hide.tabs = NULL, defaults = NULL)

Each module also ships a standalone *App() convenience function, and sciModuleGalleryApp() puts every module in one app (see below).

Note that this package sets no LazyData, so the bundled example datasets need a data() call before you can use them by name:

library(sciVizModules)
data(airway_deseq2)
data(example_sce)
data(survival_lung)

Working with an AI coding agent

sciVizModules builds on VizModules, which ships three agent skills describing its APIs. Install them into your project once and any compatible agent (Claude Code, GitHub Copilot, OpenAI Codex) will discover them:

VizModules::use_vizmodules_skills(".", client = "claude")  # or "agents" / "copilot"

Point your agent at the one that matches the job:

  • Putting sciVizModules modules into an app (defaults, hide.inputs / hide.tabs, createModuleApp(), the data filter, the Figure Builder, source-data export): vizmodules-app. It also carries a generated inventory of every VizModules module’s column-mapping keys, colour key and tab names, which the wrapper modules here inherit.
  • Building your own module on top of one of these, or of a VizModules base module (adding inputs, transforming the data before it is plotted, driving the wrapped module’s parameters): vizmodules-custom-module. Most of sciVizModules is built exactly this way, so its modules are good worked examples.
  • Writing a module from scratch around your own plotting function: vizmodules-custom-module for the Shiny wiring, plus vizmodules-new-module for the full *InputsUI() / *OutputUI() / *Server() / *App() layout, documentation and tests. The latter is written for contributions to VizModules itself, but the structure carries over.

The skills are copied from your installed VizModules, so re-run the call with overwrite = TRUE after upgrading it. AGENTS.md in the sciVizModules repository covers the conventions specific to this package on top of those.

The module gallery

To preview every module in one place, launch the gallery:

library(sciVizModules)
sciModuleGalleryApp()

Every module has its own tab, grouped into menus by field (Expression, Enrichment, Single-cell, PCA, Genomics, Mutations, Clinical, Pharmacology, Structure). Each opens on an example dataset with the module’s main features switched on: labelled genes on the volcano and MA plots, lead variants on the Manhattan and QQ plots, a risk table and median survival on the Kaplan-Meier curves, an untreated-to-treated trajectory on the sample PCA, terminal elimination fits on the PK profiles, and so on. Every control can still be changed from the tab’s sidebar, a Docs link opens the module’s reference page, and beneath the plot sits either a filterable table of the data feeding it or a read-only preview of the object it is bound to. The Overview page lists the modules as cards, and the Figure Builder tab composes several of them into one figure (see “Multi-panel figures” below).

A module’s server starts the first time its tab is opened, so the gallery launches quickly, and modules whose optional packages are not installed are left out, their Overview cards naming the packages to install.

The settings each tab opens on are the ones the module’s *App() opens on too, so passing the same defaults to a module in your own app reproduces any of them. For deployment to a Shiny server, shinyapps.io or Posit Connect, the same app ships as an app.R:

runApp(system.file("apps/module-gallery", package = "sciVizModules"))

Drop a module into your app

All modules follow the same pattern: *InputsUI() for controls, *OutputUI() for the plot, and *Server() for the logic. Here is a minimal volcano plot using the bundled airway_deseq2 differential-expression results:

library(sciVizModules)

ui <- fluidPage(
    sidebarLayout(
        sidebarPanel(
            volcanoPlotInputsUI("de",
                airway_deseq2,
                defaults = list(
                    sig.thresh = 0.05,
                    fc.thresh = 1
                )
            )
        ),
        mainPanel(volcanoPlotOutputUI("de"))
    )
)

server <- function(input, output, session) {
    volcanoPlotServer("de", data = reactive(airway_deseq2))
}

shinyApp(ui, server)

Try a module standalone

The fastest way to explore a single module is its *App() function. Called with no data, each opens on the same example dataset and showcase settings as its gallery tab:

if (interactive()) volcanoPlotApp()     # differential expression, airway_deseq2
if (interactive()) dittoDimPlotApp()    # single-cell reduction, example_sce
if (interactive()) doseResponseApp()    # pharmacology, dose_response
if (interactive()) cnSegmentPlotApp()   # copy number, example_cn_segment
if (interactive()) forestPlotApp()      # Cox / logistic / linear model, survival_lung
if (interactive()) pcaBiplotApp()       # PCAtools pca object, example_pca
if (interactive()) alphafoldConfidenceApp() # AlphaFold DB prediction for p53
if (interactive()) manhattanPlotApp()   # GWAS summary statistics, example_gwas
if (interactive()) gseaEnrichmentPlotApp() # fgsea example ranks and pathways
if (interactive()) crisprScreenRankApp() # simulated MAGeCK gene summary
if (interactive()) rocCurveApp()        # diagnostic markers, example_biomarkers
if (interactive()) pkConcentrationTimeApp() # oral theophylline, datasets::Theoph
if (interactive()) plateHeatmapApp()    # two 384-well plates, example_plate
if (interactive()) structureViewerApp() # 3D AlphaFold model of p53
if (interactive()) mdTrajectoryMetricsApp() # simulated GROMACS RMSD, Rg and RMSF
if (interactive()) oncoPlotApp()        # somatic mutations, maftools' TCGA LAML
if (interactive()) mutationalProfileApp() # simulated SBS96 spectra, example_sbs96
if (interactive()) samplePCAApp()       # bulk RNA-seq counts, the airway package
if (interactive()) deHeatmapApp()       # airway with its DESeq2 results (airway_deseq2)
if (interactive()) dittoDotPlotApp()    # marker dot plot, example_sce

Every *App() also takes defaults, hide.inputs and hide.tabs. With the example data, a key you set in defaults replaces its showcase value and the rest of the showcase stays; with your own data, only your defaults apply:

if (interactive()) survivalCurveApp(defaults = list(group.by = "ph.ecog"))
if (interactive()) survivalCurveApp(list(lung = survival_lung), hide.tabs = "Legend")

Set defaults and hide controls

Pass a named defaults list to pre-fill inputs, and use hide.inputs / hide.tabs to trim the control panel. Hidden inputs still pass their values to the plot, so the module stays fully configured.

volcanoPlotServer(
    "de",
    data        = reactive(airway_deseq2),
    defaults    = list(sig.thresh = 0.01, fc.thresh = 1),
    hide.inputs = c("shape.by"),
    hide.tabs   = c("Legend")
)

Hidden inputs and tabs still feed their values into the plot, so the module stays fully configured while exposing only what your users need.

The tab names come from the module being wrapped, so check its help page before naming one: a hide.tabs entry that matches nothing is silently ignored. For the volcano and MA modules the tabs are those of VizModules::dittoViz_scatterPlotInputsUI() – Data, Adjustments, Points, Colors, Facet, Annotations, Legend, Trajectory, Marginals, Lines, Axes, Plotly, Extras. The vizmodules-app agent skill (see above) lists the tab names and defaults keys of every VizModules base module in its module inventory.

Group colours are a defaults entry too. The volcano and MA modules assemble color.up / color.down / color.ns into the wrapped module’s color.panel mapping, so the colours open where you asked and stay editable on its Colors tab:

volcanoPlotServer(
    "de",
    data     = reactive(airway_deseq2),
    defaults = list(color.up = "#D55E00", color.down = "#0072B2")
)

App factory with createModuleApp()

The data-frame modules’ *App() functions (e.g. volcanoPlotApp(), survivalCurveApp()) are thin wrappers around VizModules’ createModuleApp(), which returns a full standalone app with data import, a filterable data table, and dataset switching for any module:

library(sciVizModules)

app <- VizModules::createModuleApp(
    inputs_ui_fn = volcanoPlotInputsUI,
    output_ui_fn = volcanoPlotOutputUI,
    server_fn    = volcanoPlotServer,
    data_list    = list("Airway DESeq2" = airway_deseq2),
    title        = "My Volcano Plot"
)
if (interactive()) runApp(app)

The vizmodules-app agent skill covers createModuleApp() and its data filter in more depth.

The data-frame modules take a data_list; the dittoSeq single-cell modules take an object_list of SingleCellExperiment / Seurat / SummarizedExperiment objects instead:

if (interactive()) {
    dittoDimPlotApp(object_list = list("Example SCE" = example_sce))
}

Data format for each module

sciVizModules modules split into two families by input type: data-frame modules and dittoSeq / single-cell modules. Every module below has a bundled example dataset you can inspect (e.g. head(airway_deseq2)).

Differential expression

Module Server function Data type Expected data Example data
Volcano plot volcanoPlotServer() data.frame Effect-size column (e.g. log2FoldChange) and a significance column (e.g. padj) airway_deseq2
MA plot maPlotServer() data.frame Mean-abundance column (baseMean / logCPM / AveExpr) and an effect-size column (log2FoldChange / logFC) airway_deseq2

Column names differ between DE tools (airway_deseq2, airway_edger, airway_voom are all bundled). The modules auto-detect common conventions, and you can override the mapping via defaults (e.g. defaults = list(x.by = "logFC", y.by = "logCPM")).

head(airway_deseq2)
#> baseMean, log2FoldChange, lfcSE, stat, pvalue, padj, symbol, ensembl

GO / functional enrichment

Module Server function Data type Expected data Example data
Enrichment dot plot enrichmentDotPlotServer() data.frame clusterProfiler-style table: a grouping column, a Description term column, a "count/total" GeneRatio string, and a p-value column example_enrichment
GO fan (sunburst) plot goFanPlotServer() data.frame GO enrichment results with a GO-ID column (auto-detected), an ontology (BP/CC/MF), and a numeric fill column (e.g. qvalue) example_enrichment

For the dot plot, dot size encodes the parsed GeneRatio and color encodes .

head(example_enrichment)
#> Cluster, ONTOLOGY, ID, Description, GeneRatio, BgRatio, pvalue, p.adjust, qvalue, Count

Survival analysis

Module Server function Data type Expected data Example data
Kaplan-Meier curve survivalCurveServer() data.frame Numeric follow-up time column and a status event column (survival::Surv() convention: 1 = censored, 2 = event); optional grouping column for stratified curves survival_lung 
head(survival_lung)
#> time, status, age, sex, ph.ecog

Comparing three or more groups

The log-rank p-value on the plot is a global test: it says whether survival differs anywhere among the groups, not which groups differ. With three or more groups, Pairwise Comparisons (pairwise = TRUE) also tests each pair, lists the adjusted p-values on the plot, shows each pair’s hazard ratio on hover, and adds the full comparison table to the source download.

fig <- survivalCurve(survival_lung,
    time = "time", status = "status", group.by = "ph.ecog",
    pairwise = TRUE, p.adjust.method = "holm"
)
attr(fig, "pairwise")
#> group1, group2, n1, n2, events1, events2, test, chisq, p.value, p.adj,
#> p.adjust.method, hr, hr.lower, hr.upper

Points to keep in mind when reading them:

  • Each pair is tested on its own subjects, with a log-rank test of the two groups (as survminer’s pairwise_survdiff() computes).
  • The p-values are adjusted for the number of comparisons made. Holm, the default, keeps the chance of any false positive among them at the nominal level. BH controls the false discovery rate instead, which suits screening many groups, and none overstates significance. Testing fewer, pre-specified comparisons (Comparisons, e.g. each group against a control) costs less power. The adjustment covers only the comparisons in this run: picking them after looking at the curves, or regrouping the data until something is significant, is not accounted for.
  • A p-value is not the size of a difference. The hazard ratio is group2 relative to group1, from a Cox model of the pair. Above 1, group2 has the higher hazard, and so shorter survival. Its 95% interval is not adjusted for multiplicity, and it can disagree slightly with the log-rank p-value near the significance cut-off.
  • The log-rank test assumes proportional hazards. It is most sensitive when one group’s hazard is a constant multiple of the other’s. Curves that cross can hide a real difference, and the hazard ratio then averages over opposite effects, so read the tests against the curves.
  • Small groups give unreliable results. In survival_lung, ph.ecog’s “In bed >50%” group is a single subject, yet its comparisons come out “significant”. Check each pair’s subjects and events (n1, n2, events1, events2), and drop or merge sparse groups (the data table filter) before testing.
  • These are unadjusted comparisons of unordered groups. For ordered groups (stage, dose), a trend test is more powerful. For the effect of a group allowing for other covariates, fit a Cox model with forestPlot().

Clinical models

Module Server function Data type Expected data Example data
Forest plot forestPlotServer() data.frame Raw data: for a Cox model a time and an event column (as for the survival curve); for a logistic model a binary outcome; for a linear model a numeric outcome; plus any numeric or categorical covariates. The module fits the model survival_lung
ROC curve rocCurveServer() data.frame One row per subject: a binary outcome column and one or more numeric predictor columns example_biomarkers 
forestPlot(survival_lung,
    model = "cox", time = "time", status = "status",
    covariates = c("age", "sex", "ph.ecog")
)
data(example_biomarkers)
roc <- rocCurve(example_biomarkers, response = "disease",
    predictors = c("marker_strong", "marker_moderate", "marker_weak"))
attr(roc, "table")  # AUC, CI and Youden cut-off per predictor

Biochemical kinetics and pharmacology

Module Server function Data type Expected data Example data
Michaelis-Menten michaelisMentenServer() reactive list A list with data (observed-points data.frame), model (fitted-line data.frame), and optional stats (an nls fit or named K / Vmax coefficients for annotation) mm_kinetics, mm_kinetics_line, mm_kinetics_fit
Dose-response doseResponseServer() data.frame A dose column (plotted on a log10 scale) and a response column; the module fits a log-logistic curve with drc dose_response
PK concentration-time pkConcentrationTimeServer() data.frame One row per sample: subject, time and concentration columns, optionally a dose and a treatment group (Subject/ID, Time/TAD, conc/DV, Dose/AMT are detected) datasets::Theoph

The Michaelis-Menten module consumes pre-computed pieces rather than a single data frame:

str(list(
    data  = mm_kinetics,       # columns S (substrate), v (velocity)
    model = mm_kinetics_line,  # predicted S, v over a fine grid
    stats = mm_kinetics_fit    # nls fit -> supplies K and Vmax
))
head(dose_response)
#> dose_uM, rep1_response_pct, ..., mean_response_pct, sd_response_pct

The PK module computes each subject’s non-compartmental parameters the way PKNCA does by default (linear-up / log-down AUC, best-fit terminal slope):

pk <- pkConcentrationTime(datasets::Theoph, time = "Time", conc = "conc",
    subject = "Subject", dose = "Dose", log.y = TRUE, show.lambda = TRUE)
head(attr(pk, "table"))  # Cmax, Tmax, AUClast, half-life, AUCinf, CL/F, Vz/F

Screening and plate assays

Module Server function Data type Expected data Example data
Plate heatmap plateHeatmapServer() data.frame One row per well: a well identifier (A01, B7, AF48), a numeric readout, and optionally a plate column and a column labelling the positive and negative control wells example_plate 
data(example_plate)
head(example_plate)
plateHeatmap(example_plate, well = "well", value = "signal", plate = "plate",
    control = "type", positive = "positive", negative = "negative",
    normalise = "bscore", marginals = TRUE)

Copy number

Module Server function Data type Expected data Example data
Copy-number segments cnSegmentPlotServer() CNSegment, or a named list of them A CNSegment object as returned by sesame::cnSegmentation(): bin-level log2 signal ratios in bin.signals, their coordinates in bin.coords, and a genomeInfo carrying cytoBand (for chromosome ticks and centromere guides) and optionally genes (for labels) example_cn_segment

Passing a named list plots one panel per sample, stacked over a shared genomic x-axis. Like the PCAtools and AlphaFold modules, it does not take a data frame, so it cannot go in the Figure Builder.

data(example_cn_segment)
example_cn_segment

GWAS QQ plot gwasQQPlotServer() data.frame Summary statistics with a p-value column example_gwas

Module Server function Data type Expected data Example data

Functional genomics screens

Module Server function Data type Expected data Example data
CRISPR screen rank crisprScreenRankServer() data.frame A MAGeCK RRA (mageck test) or MLE (mageck mle) gene_summary.txt, read with read_mageck() simulated, in inst/extdata 
screen <- read_mageck(system.file("extdata", "example_mageck.gene_summary.txt.gz",
    package = "sciVizModules"))
head(screen)

# An MLE summary carries one beta, z-score and FDR per condition; the module
# plots one condition at a time.
mle <- read_mageck(system.file("extdata", "example_mageck_mle.gene_summary.txt.gz",
    package = "sciVizModules"))
head(mle)

Somatic mutations

Module Server function Data type Expected data Example data
Oncoplot oncoPlotServer() data.frame or maftools MAF Variants in MAF columns: Hugo_Symbol, Tumor_Sample_Barcode, Variant_Classification, and a protein-change column (HGVSp_Short, Protein_Change or AAChange); columns constant within a sample are its annotations maftools’ TCGA LAML
MAF summary mafSummaryServer() data.frame or maftools MAF As above, plus Variant_Type, Reference_Allele and Tumor_Seq_Allele2 for the type and substitution panels maftools’ TCGA LAML
Mutation lollipop mutationLollipopServer() data.frame or maftools MAF As above; domains from maftools when installed, or the server’s domains argument maftools’ TCGA LAML
SBS96 spectrum mutationalProfileServer() matrix or data.frame 96-channel substitution counts: 96 x samples (MutationalPatterns mut_matrix()), samples x 96 (maftools trinucleotideMatrix()$nmf_matrix), or a channel column plus one column per sample example_sbs96

Silent variants are dropped as maftools::read.maf() drops them; the gene, sample and substitution summaries match maftools’.

# The TCGA LAML cohort maftools ships, with its clinical annotations.
laml <- read.delim(system.file("extdata", "tcga_laml.maf.gz", package = "maftools"),
    comment.char = "#")
clinical <- read.delim(system.file("extdata", "tcga_laml_annot.tsv", package = "maftools"))
laml <- merge(laml, clinical, by = "Tumor_Sample_Barcode")
head(laml[, c("Hugo_Symbol", "Tumor_Sample_Barcode", "Variant_Classification", "Protein_Change")])
oncoPlot(laml, top.n = 15, clinical.tracks = "FAB_classification")

Bulk expression

Module Server function Data type Expected data Example data
Sample PCA samplePCAServer() SummarizedExperiment Counts (or any assay) with sample metadata in colData airway (airway package)
Sample distances sampleDistanceHeatmapServer() SummarizedExperiment As above airway (airway package)
DE heatmap deHeatmapServer() bundle list(object = <SummarizedExperiment>, results = <DE results table>), or a SummarizedExperiment whose rowData holds the results airway with airway_deseq2

Their *App() functions take a named list of experiments (or, for the DE heatmap, of bundles). The counts are transformed in the module: DESeq2’s variance-stabilising transformation when DESeq2 is installed, otherwise log2 CPM. The two heatmaps (and dittoHeatmap) wrap VizModules’ ComplexHeatmap_Heatmap module, so they are InteractiveComplexHeatmap widgets rather than plotly figures and need ComplexHeatmap, InteractiveComplexHeatmap and circlize. sample_pca() builds the same PCA for the PCAtools modules below.

data("airway", package = "airway")
airway
pcaScreePlot(sample_pca(airway, transform = "log2cpm"))

Principal component analysis (PCAtools)

Module Server function Data type Expected data Example data
Biplot pcaBiplotServer() PCAtools pca The object PCAtools::pca() returns: sample scores (rotated), variable loadings, variance explained, and sample metadata example_pca
Scree plot pcaScreePlotServer() PCAtools pca As above example_pca
Loadings plot pcaLoadingsPlotServer() PCAtools pca As above example_pca
Pairs plot pcaPairsPlotServer() PCAtools pca As above example_pca
PC-metadata correlation pcaEigencorPlotServer() PCAtools pca As above; needs sample metadata example_pca

Their *App() functions take a named pca_list. A pca object is a plain list, so the modules read it without PCAtools installed; PCAtools is needed only to make one, and to mark the elbow on the scree plot.

data(example_pca)
round(example_pca$variance, 1)
head(example_pca$metadata)

Structural biology

Module Server function Data type Expected data Example data
AlphaFold confidence alphafoldConfidenceServer() read_alphafold() result AlphaFold DB *-predicted_aligned_error_v*.json and *-confidence_v*.json, a ColabFold *_scores_*.json, or a predicted model (.pdb / .cif) whose B-factors hold the pLDDT; files may be gzipped AlphaFold DB prediction for p53 (P04637), in inst/extdata 
af <- read_alphafold(
    pae = system.file("extdata", "AF-P04637-F1-predicted_aligned_error_v6.json.gz",
        package = "sciVizModules"),
    confidence = system.file("extdata", "AF-P04637-F1-confidence_v6.json.gz",
        package = "sciVizModules")
)
af
alphafoldConfidence(af)

AlphaFold DB data is available under CC-BY 4.0; cite Jumper et al. (2021) and Varadi et al. (2024) when you use it.

Module Server function Data type Expected data Example data
3D structure viewer structureViewerServer() read_structure() result A PDB or mmCIF file (from the PDB, AlphaFold DB, ColabFold, …), optionally gzipped AlphaFold DB model of p53 (P04637), in inst/extdata
MD trajectory metrics mdTrajectoryMetricsServer() data.frame read_xvg() output from GROMACS .xvg files (gmx rms, gmx gyrate, gmx rmsf, …), several files combined with rbind(): columns x, value, series and metric simulated, in inst/extdata

structureViewer is the one module that is not a plotly figure. It is an NGL 3D widget, so it has its own PNG snapshot button instead of the Source Data download, and it is not available to the Figure Builder.

p53 <- read_structure(system.file("extdata", "AF-P04637-F1-model_v6.pdb.gz",
    package = "sciVizModules"))
p53
structureViewer(p53, color.by = "plddt", highlight = "175, 248, 273")
ext <- function(f) system.file("extdata", f, package = "sciVizModules")
md <- rbind(
    read_xvg(ext("example_rmsd_rep1.xvg.gz"), series = "replica 1"),
    read_xvg(ext("example_rmsd_rep2.xvg.gz"), series = "replica 2")
)
mdTrajectoryMetrics(md, smooth.window = 25, time.unit = "ps to ns")

Single-cell / RNA-seq (dittoSeq wrappers)

These modules wrap dittoSeq plotting functions. They all accept a SingleCellExperiment, Seurat, or SummarizedExperiment object and take object_list (rather than data_list) in their *App() functions. The bundled example_sce (a simulated SingleCellExperiment with PCA/TSNE/UMAP reductions and both discrete and continuous metadata) works with all of them.

All of these take the same data type: a SingleCellExperiment, Seurat, or SummarizedExperiment object.

Module Server function Purpose
Dimensional reduction dittoDimPlotServer() Cells in a reduction (UMAP/t-SNE/PCA), colored by a gene or metadata
Hex-binned reduction dittoDimHexServer() Hex-binned version of the dim plot for dense embeddings
Scatter dittoScatterPlotServer() Two continuous variables, optional third for color
Distribution dittoPlotServer() A continuous variable across groups (jitter / violin / box / ridge)
Ridge + jitter dittoRidgeJitterServer() Ridge plots with overlaid jitter
Composition bar dittoBarPlotServer() Discrete composition per group (percent or count)
Frequency dittoFreqPlotServer() Per-sample frequencies of a discrete variable across groups
Dot plot dittoDotPlotServer() Marker genes: mean expression (colour) and fraction expressing (size) per group
Heatmap dittoHeatmapServer() Expression of chosen genes across cells, with metadata annotations (an InteractiveComplexHeatmap widget) 
data(example_sce)
example_sce

Multi-panel figures

The data-frame modules are registered with the VizModules Figure Builder, so several panels can be dragged, sized and exported as one figure. It is also the last tab of the module gallery:

sciFigureBuilderApp()

sci_figure_builder_registry() returns the registry itself, in the shape VizModules::figureBuilderServer() documents, so you can extend it with your own modules. Its entries come from the same registry as the gallery, so a panel opens on its gallery tab’s settings when its example dataset is the one picked:

registry <- sci_figure_builder_registry()
names(registry)
str(registry$volcano, max.level = 1)

The vizmodules-app agent skill covers embedding the Figure Builder in your own app, and vizmodules-custom-module covers building a module to register in it.

mutationalProfile is registered alongside the differential-expression, enrichment, dose-response and survival modules. The dittoSeq modules, the bulk expression modules, cnSegmentPlot, michaelisMenten, the PCAtools modules, gseaEnrichmentPlot and alphafoldConfidence are not: the builder’s dataset catalogue holds data frames, and those take other objects. structureViewer is a 3D widget rather than a plotly figure. forestPlot, the GWAS modules, crisprScreenRank, the MAF modules (oncoPlot, mafSummary, mutationLollipop), rocCurve, pkConcentrationTime, plateHeatmap and mdTrajectoryMetrics are not registered yet.

Export the source data

Every module’s control panel ends in a Source Data button. It downloads a ZIP holding a self-contained interactive HTML of the plot, an SVG and a PNG of it as drawn on screen, a CSV of the data actually plotted, a CSV of the UI input values, and a statistics table where the module computes one. The Figure Builder writes one such set per panel, named after the panel label.

This is plumbed by VizModules::collect_source_data() and VizModules::create_source_download_handler(), which every module here already wires up, so nothing is needed on your side. Two notes:

  • The SVG and PNG are photographed in the browser off the graph you are looking at, so they carry anything applied after the figure was built. The button therefore pauses briefly before the archive arrives.
  • The interactive HTML needs pandoc (via htmlwidgets::saveWidget()). Without it the archive still downloads, with a warning and no HTML.

Which plot parameters are exposed?

Modules wrap plotting functions from dittoViz, plotthis, dittoSeq, and several specialized packages. To see which arguments a module surfaces:

  1. Open the module input help page, e.g., ?volcanoPlotInputsUI or ?dittoDimPlotInputsUI. The Details section notes which arguments from the underlying plot function are wired through and any that are intentionally omitted.
  2. Cross-reference the base plot documentation (?dittoSeq::dittoDimPlot, etc.). Input names in defaults line up with those function arguments when they are supported.

If an argument is listed as missing or non-functional in the module docs, it has been intentionally hidden because it does not round-trip well in the interactive Plotly output.

Contributing a module

Every module in sciVizModules is in the gallery. A module’s entry in the gallery’s registry (.sci_module_showcase() in R/module_showcase.R) is part of the module: it gives the module its gallery tab, the example its *App() opens on, and, for a data-frame module, its Figure Builder entry, with showcase settings that switch on the features the module is worth reaching for. The test suite derives the package’s modules from its exports and fails when one has no entry, or when an entry’s settings name a column, value or control that does not exist, so a new module cannot ship without a working gallery tab. AGENTS.md in the repository walks through the steps.
